rationale: B wins because it makes the missing reliability number the story, not just a caveat: “Replit's new agent builds and ships working apps for people who can't code — and won't say how often they break.” A sees the same issue but buries it under proof needs: “Without at least one of these, the category claim is a press release.” That is disciplined, but it leaves the sharpest reporter question sitting on the bench.
gaps_in_A: A misses the strongest standalone angle in the update: reliability is undisclosed. It notes “how often generated apps work without fixes” as proof, but never turns that into the dev-tools testing story.

“Replit bets its next users will never write a line of code” overstates the supplied facts. The update says Replit positions the agent for non-engineers and vibe coders, not that its next growth cohort will never code.
“charges for the work, not the seat” is too neat. The facts say usage-based pricing sits on top of subscriptions; they do not prove Replit is replacing seat pricing.
gaps_in_B: “CS teachers are already arguing about” and “this school year” add a plausible classroom frame, but they are not in the supplied update. Useful color, sloppy sourcing.
The customer-story angle admits its own hole: “without one, this is a product blurb.” No named non-engineer user was supplied, so calling it one of “four viable angles” is generous.
“you have four viable angles but no current signal” is the wrong next-step diagnosis. The launch is the current signal; the real missing piece is proof, especially reliability and named users.
“the whole software industry is arguing about” is oversized. The pricing angle is real, but that line inflates one Replit pricing fact into an industry-wide fight without evidence.
